newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Mandela starts Asia visit to learn from Tigers.
newsitem.headline: Mandela starts Asia visit to learn from Tigers.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela launched his Asian tour with a visit to the Philippines on Saturday, and said he hoped to learn from the region's "Tiger" economies on how to raise the living conditions of his own people.

Accompanied for the first time on a state visit by his Mozambican female companion, Mandela immediately plunged into talks with President Fidel Ramos and met fellow freedom fighter, former president Corazon Aquino.

"This part of the world has made fantastic achievements economically and politically...I have looked forward to coming to this region because of the enormous lessons which we can learn in trying to raise the living conditions of our people," Mandela said in a press conference after his talks with Ramos.
He said his country could learn much from the vibrant economies of members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

"We in southern Africa are looking forward to the deepening of relations between ASEAN and the Southern African Development Community," he said in the prepared text of a speech he was to deliver later on Saturday at a state banquet hosted by Ramos.
"The will is there. The geographic and political conditions make this opportune. The social and economic challenges dictate it," he added.

Mandela also met with Aquino whom he hailed as an inspiration to the world. Aquino led the peaceful "people power" revolt in 1986 which ousted the 20-year regime of former strongman Ferdinand Marcos and inspired democracy movements elsewhere in the world.
Mandela, 78, and his companion Graca Machel, the 51-year-old widow of former Mozambican president Somora Machel, were greeted by a 21-gun salute and full military honours.
Ramos called Mandela "one of the towering figures of the century".
"His struggle changed the face of race relations across the world," Ramos told a news conference.
Mandela introduced Graca, dressed in maroon and gold, as his "companion" to Ramos, who smiled and shook hands with her.

Asked by a reporter later if a wedding was in the offing, Mandela said: "My cultural background does not permit me to discuss this question with people young enough to be my children or grandchildren".

Mandela was divorced from his second wife Winnie last year after a bitter court battle in which he acknowledged she had been unfaithful to him. His first wife Evelyn lives in the rural south coast Transkei, where he has built a retirement home.
Mandela and Graca have said they have no plans to marry.
South African and Philippine officials signed an agreement to expand cooperation in trade and investment and to grant each other "Most Favoured Nation" status in trade relations.
Ramos said investment links between the two countries could include projects in the energy, mining and railway sectors but details still had to be worked out.
On Sunday, Mandela will address members of the Makati Business Club, the country's premier group of businessmen.
He leaves for Brunei on Monday and will visit Malaysia and Singapore before returning to South Africa.
